headline: 30 YEARS, 3 DIRECTORS, 1 CITY: DELHI
text: Delhi isn’t just a backdrop; it has often been quite a strong character in cinema — with its stories, layers, language, and locations, making its presence felt. Filmmakers say Delhi is often a co-writer in ﬁlms, like the most iconic cinematic cities. Filmmakers, such as Sudhir Mishra, Vishal Bhardwaj, Rajkumar Hirani, Anurag Kashyap, Imtiaz Ali, Shoojit Sircar, Shekhar Kapur, Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra, Kabir Khan, Mira Nair and Richie Mehta, have stitched its character into their ﬁlms, shot here, or narrated the stories of the city. In the recent years, Rahul Chitella captured a bungalow in Delhi as a memory-keeper in Gulmohar. Vidhu Vinod Chopra’s 12th Fail zeroed in on the grinding nature of Mukherjee Nagar. In these ﬁlms, Delhi is as much about space as it is about the people who ﬁll it. Lately, streaming platforms have captured many untouched Delhi stories — the cops in Paatal Lok and Delhi Crime, the Uphaar cinema tragedy in Trial by Fire, and a wedding-mad Delhi in Made in Heaven. Delhi as a shooting location has fascinated ﬁlmmakers as much as its stories. We spoke to three directors, who have put Delhi locations and stories on the map, about their ﬁlming experiences in the capital. Raj Kumar Hirani A still Raj Kumar Hirani's PK Three Idiots People would land up at night with dabbas to watch PK’s shooting at Connaught Place: Raj Kumar Hirani Delhi, I feel, has far more interesting locations than we have in Mumbai today. Mumbai, of course, has the sea, but Delhi has a lot of historical sites and monuments, and I wanted to include that in my ﬁlms. We shot at Humayun’s Tomb and Agrasen ki Baoli for PK. We shot across Delhi in different areas, and one of the locations I clearly remember was CP. We shot for two nights in CP, where PK meets Sardarji, and that one place used to get really crowded. People would land up at night with dabbas and stay to watch the shooting, but it was well organised. The whole worry for us was how we would shoot with Aamir on the streets, but it happened very peacefully. In fact, for 3 Idiots, we shot with Aamir and Kareena in the exact same location where we later shot for PK. Whenever I meet someone from Delhi, they often talk about PK; I guess people in Delhi really liked the ﬁlm. Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra Delhi 6 A still from Rang De Basanti What, where and how I have captured Delhi the answer is in my movies: Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra I have grown up in Delhi. The whole area around the Rashtrapati Bhawan, Rajpath, and Janpath has been in my subconscious all the time. When you grow up in a city, it has a different meaning for you. I have shot three ﬁlms that have featured Delhi. Delhi-6, which is about my growing years. My nani and dadi used to live in Old Delhi. Bhaag Milkha Bhaag had the National Stadium scenes, to show Milkha Singh’s training in Delhi. We also shot at the cantonment as he was a jawan in the Army. The way I see Delhi is that it is the heart of the country. It’s not just a political centre; it has the Supreme Court and the Parliament. The various pillars of democracy — the Legislature, the Executive, the judiciary and the Press — are in Delhi. Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg houses all the newspaper ofﬁces and is dubbed the Fleet Street of India. Delhi is also a conﬂuence of (states) UP, MP, Rajasthan, and Himachal. It’s a melting pot for northern India. And, of course, people from all over India, who are in the services, live in Delhi. All Defence services have their headquarters, and all the ministers, who are representatives of the people of the country, reside and work there. Certainly, we can’t do without Delhi. It’s very different when we talk about Delhi as a location — that kind of belittles its importance. Locations can be sand dunes or deserts of Morocco, but for me, Delhi holds much more importance — it is intangible. I’m a Delhi boy; you can’t take Delhi out of me. What, where, and how I have captured Delhi — the answer lies in my movies. My craving for the culture of Delhi is something I try to capture through ﬁlms. Fortunately for me, as a ﬁlmmaker and a writer, I can choose to write stories about the city. Raj Kumar Gupta No One Killed Jessica The first montage dialogue in NOKJ sums up the city: Raj Kumar Gupta It is strange with Delhi — you love the city, but you are also kind of looking over your shoulder. For me, the ﬁrst montage dialogue in No One Killed Jessica (NOKJ) sums up the city (In the monologue Rani Mukerji says that she has never understood Delhi — ‘Har jhagde ke shuru mein har aadmi kehta hai janta nahi main kaun hoon? Everybody is somebody in Delhi. Nobody is a nobody’). It is a very fascinating and cinematic city. In Delhi, most people have seen No One Killed Jessica. They keep bringing up the ﬁlm, and it is something that touched them because they were kind of part of the story. It affected the city, and the subject resonated across the country. Whenever I’m in Delhi, it brings back memories of shooting the ﬁlm. We shot across Delhi for NOKJ and after that, I shot for Raid, for a few days, and then we shot extensively for the web series Pill, at different locations in the capital, including Old Delhi. Last year, when I came to Delhi for a shoot, I stayed in a place next to the cemetery (opposite Taj Mansingh), where we had ﬁlmed scenes for NOKJ. When one is shooting, it’s a different mindset, but later, during every visit, I keep thinking — we shot that scene here.

headline: OTT shows decode Delhi’s diversity
text: One would assume that a comedy about living independently, a satire on the lavish lifestyles of the elite, and a true-crime story of the most horrific gang-rape in recent memory would have nothing in common. However, the three do have one thematic connection – their geographical setting is Delhi. With the proliferation of web content over the last few years, there have been many shows set in the national capital. Filmmakers say that Delhi, as a location, offers contrastingly different landscape and architecture, ranging from small bylanes to broad highways and from crowded slums to plush localities and high-rises. This means that shows set in Delhi are not just diverse in terms of locales but also themes and genres. The creative minds behind the various OTT shows set and shot in the capital tell us what makes Delhi so easy to depict in such diverse and new ways. Existence of diverse stories in Delhi Even as multiple OTT shows have been based in Delhi, almost all of them show starkly different shades of the capital. Reema Kagti , one of the co-creators of Made in Heaven, called Delhi “the wedding capital of India” while promoting the show in 2019. The show tells the story of two wedding planners handling the nuptials of Delhi’s filthy rich. The show’s other co-creator Zoya Akhtar added, “Delhi is a beautiful place to shoot. It’s differently cinematic. For the kind of story that we wanted to tell, we needed spaces like that.” But Delhi was equally fitting as a setting for the Emmy Award-winning Delhi Crime, the show inspired from Delhi Police’s investigation of the infamous 2012 Delhi gang-rape. Rajesh Tailang, who played one of the policemen in the show, argues that even if it was a fictional tale, it would have been set in the capital. “Of course, this show had to be set in Delhi. The incident which inspired this show took place in Delhi. But even if it was a fictional show, this would have made sense being set in Delhi. It’s not as if women are only unsafe in Delhi but if you ask me for a comparative between Delhi and Mumbai, I’d say the problem of women being unsafe in an urban metropolis while venturing out at night is associated more with Delhi,” he says. ‘Longer runtime on OTT allows us to show newer parts of Delhi’ The depiction of Delhi in OTT shows has moved away from how the city was portrayed in cinema over the years. Instead of shots of India Gate or Qutub Minar that cinema had often employed to depict Delhi, web shows are moving beyond these usual suspects to depict newer parts of Delhi that had never found their way on to screens. Filmmakers and writers attribute this to the longer run time that web series offer as opposed to feature films. “When you’re narrating a long format story, as a creator, you’re aware that you have the advantage of runtime. Hence, it doesn’t become too important to establish a city via the typical or iconic locations,” says Mayank Sharma , creator and director of Breathe: Into The Shadows. The series showcases neighbourhoods, roads and bylanes of various parts of Delhi, shot almost exclusively during the winters. Mayank adds, “What I find interesting is for us to invest and spend time to show different settings and locations of Delhi that people have probably not seen or experienced yet. An unexplored or a new location demands shots that have to be contrived entirely from scratch, which brings freshness to the storytelling.” ‘Delhi carries a lot of cities within itself’ Even when some of the Delhi-based stories are similar thematically, a mere shift in geographical setting within Delhi makes them tonally different. So, while Made in Heaven and Shaadi Boys both deal with wedding planning, the former deals with the weddings of Delhi’s ultra-wealthy elites, the latter is set around west Delhi’s middle class shaadis. Filmmakers add that this diversity across Delhi allows them to retain the individuality of stories. “The representation of Delhi in Indian cinema has either been tinted with a lens of nostalgia or set around almost a make-believe upper middle-class west Delhi world. But even though the cinematic representation has been two-dimensional, Delhi is not one city. It carries a lot of cities within itself. It carries a lot of different kinds of lives and cultures within itself,” argues Sudip Sharma , creator and co-writer of Pataal Lok . The crime thriller follows a cop from ‘Jamuna paar’ – the part of Delhi that seldom finds cinematic mention. “In Delhi, they look at you a certain way if you are from a certain area,” continues Sudip, “You are immediately boxed in. Depending on whether your answer to the question ‘where are you from’ is Vasant Kunj or Patparganj, you are looked at differently. Where you set the story sets it apart from another story with a similar theme.” ‘Authenticity key while setting a show in Delhi’ Creators say that authenticity becomes important when setting a story in a real place, in this case Delhi, particularly for the web medium. “Unlike a movie, which caters to a family crowd, web series are mostly consumed by individuals. Most people watch it on their laptops. They expect it to be real. So, the tone and language need to convey the same,” says Siddharth Singh, co-writer of Shaadi Boys, one of the first OTT shows set in Delhi. And the creative minds behind these shows say they are willing to take extra pains to showcase Delhi as authentically as possible. While shooting for Breathe: Into The Shadows, Mayank and his crew made sure they shot at Delhi’s Ramlila. He elaborates, “We made sure that while the Ramlila mela was happening in Delhi, I flew with my core team and we captured the authentic visuals from the actual event itself, which added a lot to the authenticity of the scene, showcasing the way people celebrate that festival. Today’s audience can quickly make out the difference between what’s real and what’s made up. Hence, hands-on research is pivotal for realistic and engrossing storytelling.”

headline: Shoot at site! Why Delhi may soon become film hub
text: NEW DELHI: To make Delhi a global destination for film production, attract tourism and ensure that filmmakers don't have to run around for clearances, the Arvind Kejriwal government on Friday launched Delhi Film Policy 2022. The new policy will ensure all approvals and clearances to shoot a film in Delhi are electronically provided within 15 days and production houses hiring local talent will get subsidy. Delhi would also have its own film festival, as grand as the one organised in Cannes in France, and film excellence awards where crew members would be felicitated for their contribution. The government said it would send a delegation of Delhi Tourism and Transportation Development Corporation (DTTDC) to Cannes Film Festival and take experience to help them prepare the outline for Delhi International Film Festival. While the cabinet had given its approval to the policy in February, deputy CM Manish Sisodia, who also holds the portfolio of tourism department, formally launched it on Friday. The policy will come into effect with a gazette notification in a couple of days. Sisodia said Delhi Film Policy 2022 would also create massive employment and economic development opportunities in Delhi, along with attracting tourism. "The policy will help Delhi evolve as a brand, with more coverage on the silver screen and instil a sense of pride among Delhiites. The policy will bring together the entire world of hospitality, tourism, transport, cinema and artistes. It is a progressive policy prepared after studying film promotion and tourism policies at the global level," he added. Filmmakers shooting in Delhi and hiring local people will get a subsidy in the expenses incurred in making the film. The subsidy amount will be calculated on the basis of points system allocated for choosing a film location, branding of the location, involvement of local artists in the film crew and support staff and expenses during pre-production, production and post-production. The government has set aside Rs 30 crore for Delhi Film Fund. A single window e-film clearance portal has been set up on the website of Delhi Tourism, where filmmakers will be able to get approval from the required agencies based on their location within just 15 days. If early approval is needed, filmmakers will have to pay a premium. Officials said there are 25 agencies, including Archaeological Survey of India, Delhi Metro, Delhi International Airport Limited, National Highway Authority, authorities of Lotus Temple and Iskcon Temple apart from Delhi Police, traffic police and civic bodies available on the online clearance portal. DTTDC will be the nodal agency for implementing this policy and services. "All these agencies are now onboard the single platform to make Delhi a film hub at the national and international level. Regular meetings with government agencies and other stakeholders, such as production houses, were held through videoconferencing before finalising the policy," said Swati Sharma, secretary (tourism) and MD, DTTDC. The link to access the film policy and e-window clearance system is available on DTTDC's new website www.delhitourism.gov.in, which was also launched by Sisodia on Friday. Officials said filmmakers and production agencies would also get a Delhi Film Card worth Rs 1 lakh to avail of special deals and packages, including discounts on facilities like travel within Delhi, logistics and hotels, among others. The policy envisages setting up of a Film Shooting Promotion Cell, apart from a Development Cell and a Film Advisory Body to promote film production in Delhi. The new DTTDC website also contains interesting information such as "Unexplored Delhi", entertainment and fun hubs, places for children to visit, details of food and shopping hubs, biodiversity parks, etc.

headline: Delhi water crisis: Police starts patrol along Munak canal, Atishi inspects pipeline network
text: NEW DELHI: Police in Delhi initiated patrols along the Munak canal area to monitor the activities of the tanker mafia on Thursday. Concurrently, Atishi , Delhi minister, inspected the pipeline network responsible for supplying water to residents of South Delhi as the water crisis in the city intensified. According to a senior officer, police teams have established pickets and commenced patrolling the 15-kilometre stretch of the canal along the Haryana borders, which supplies water to the national capital. The canal enters Delhi from Bawana and reaches the Haiderpur Treatment Plant. Police stations in Bawana, Narela Industrial Area, Shahbad Dairy, and Samai Pur Badali have assigned teams to patrol the Munak Canal and its surrounding areas. "Police personnel have been asked to prevent anyone from taking water from the canal in their tankers," the officer said. On Wednesday, lieutenant governor V K Saxena instructed the Delhi Police chief to ensure strict vigilance along the Munak canal to prevent water theft and requested an action taken report within the week. Meanwhile, Delhi Water Minister Atishi, accompanied by senior officials of Delhi Jal Board and Revenue Department, inspected the South Delhi Mains pipeline network that supplies water from the Sonia Vihar water treatment plant to millions of people across South Delhi, she said in a post on 'X'. The plight of Delhiites, who are enduring an unprecedented high summer heat, has been further exacerbated by an acute shortage of water supply. Atishi, in her post, mentioned that the Delhi government is taking measures to prevent water wastage due to leakage from the main pipelines. This is being done through patrolling by additional district magistrates and sub-divisional magistrates across the city, ensuring that not even a single drop of water is wasted. She further stated that Delhi is currently facing a shortage of water, and the production at water treatment plants has decreased. Given these circumstances, she emphasized that water wastage will not be tolerated. During the inspection, Atishi said that water production in Delhi has decreased by 40 MGD, and the shortfall cannot be addressed unless Haryana releases more water for the city through the Yamuna.
